title: Tech-to-Owner Buyout Kit for Trade Shops
one_liner: Package and finance the sale of sub-$5M trade shops to their own senior technicians or managers, then keep them on a shared back office so the acquired shop does not stall.
customer: Retiring owners of 5-40 person HVAC, plumbing, electrical and roofing shops that PE roll-ups skip, plus their number-two techs or GMs and SBA lenders.
problem: McKinsey says 6M small businesses face ownership transitions by 2035 and a third of owners over 50 struggle to find a buyer. PE pays 10-14x EBITDA for platforms above $25M revenue but only 2-3.5x for small owner-operators, a 3-5x valuation gap. When the small shop closes, its crew and customers vanish, deepening the trades shortage.
solution: A deal factory: clean financials from QuickBooks and field-service exports, SBA 7(a) plus seller-note packaging, a 90-day transition playbook, license-qualifier continuity, and a fractional-CFO and shared back office (payroll, purchasing group, bidding) for the new owner. A short cohort teaches buyer-techs finance, hiring and pricing.
why_now: PE buying spree (Apollo/Apex, Blackstone/Champions, Bain/Service Logic) raises the visible price of scale but skips small shops. The silver-tsunami timeline is now. Roofing is the least consolidated trade and ServiceTitan is deprioritizing it, so owners have fewer software-led growth options.
revenue_model: 3-5% success fee on the deal. $2-4K per month shared back-office subscription for 24-36 months.
non_obvious_insight: The best buyer for a small shop is not PE or a stranger, it is the employee who already knows the customers, trucks and quirks. What is missing is packaging, seller financing and post-close operating support. Every closed shop deletes 5-20 tradespeople from a scarce local supply, which makes preservation valuable to the community.
first_30_days: Pick one trade in one metro. Cold-outreach 200 owners aged 58+ from state license databases with a free 30-minute valuation chat. Sign three exclusive listings, identify the tech buyers via the owners, and line up two SBA lenders.

title: Liquidity for Managers of Overheld PE Companies
one_liner: Give executives in stuck PE portfolio companies a way to cash out part of their vested equity through third-party buyers, so sponsors can fix management retention without diluting the fund or forcing an exit.
customer: Lower-middle-market PE sponsors and independent sponsors holding 2019-2021 vintage platforms. They pay for the diagnostic. Portfolio-company CEOs, CFOs and operators hold vested profits interests or options. Family offices and secondary funds supply the capital that buys management equity.
problem: Hold periods have stretched to roughly seven years. Management teams are fatigued and their incentive plans have lost value, which raises the risk they leave. The fund cannot exit (LPs tolerate little markdown), and topping up the management incentive plan (MIP) dilutes the sponsor's remaining upside.
solution: (1) A 'MIP Health Check': a waterfall model built from the operating agreement showing each manager's equity value under three exit dates and prices, with a retention-risk score. (2) A 'management tender desk': arrange third-party purchase of 10-25% of a manager's vested units at a negotiated discount, with sponsor consent and rights of first refusal, funded by a syndicate of family offices and secondary funds. (3) A cost and dilution comparison against a traditional MIP reload. Structured through a registered broker-dealer partner and securities counsel.
why_now: Bain's 2026 midyear report says most buyout assets were acquired in 2021 or earlier, the implied capital cycle is about seven years, and roughly one in five LPs are cutting buyout allocations. Bain's year-end outlook counts 32,000 unrealized companies worth $3.8T and says 40% of portfolio companies are held over 5 years, versus 29% in 2019. Fund-level returns flatten after year eight, so the pressure to retain operators through the extended hold is acute.
revenue_model: $5-10K per MIP Health Check billed to the sponsor. 1.5-3% placement fee on tender volume, paid by buyers. Later, SaaS for waterfall tracking at $1-3K/month per fund.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is human capital inside assets that cannot be sold, and the only retention lever that costs the fund nothing in dilution is third-party liquidity for managers. Bain's midyear report says: 'Stretched holding periods have fatigued management teams and depleted incentive plan value, complicating mid-hold value-creation refreshes,' and that more than half of LPs cap tolerated markdowns on full exits at 5%, which pushes GPs to hold underperformers longer (https://www.bain.com/insights/private-equity-midyear-report-2026/). 'Stretched holds' and '12 is the new 5' EBITDA growth targets (https://www.bain.com/insights/welcome-to-a-new-era-global-private-equity-report-2026/) mean operators are being asked to deliver more for longer. Employee tender offers are routine in venture-backed startups but are, by my inference, rare for PE-backed profits interests, so this looks like an open niche. That is an inference from the sources, not something they state. Regulatory structure is the main risk.
first_30_days: Build a profits-interest waterfall calculator from a standard operating-agreement template. Retain securities and tax counsel for a scoping memo and line up a registered broker-dealer partner. Offer free Health Checks to 15 independent sponsors and lower-mid-market GPs with 2019-2021 vintage assets, reached through ACG, Searchfunder and direct outreach. Then sign 2-3 paid checks at $5K and use the results to pitch one family office to fund a first tender.

title: Managed Runtime for Custom Apps Built for Local Businesses
one_liner: A white-label hosting, backup and "someone to call" layer for AI-built custom apps that freelancers and owners now build for small businesses.
customer: Two buyers. (a) Solo builders, freelancers and small agencies who build custom tools for local businesses, including failed micro-SaaS founders. They pay wholesale per app and mark it up. (b) Small business owners who built a tool themselves and want it kept alive.
problem: Builders and buyers have both moved off subscription SaaS, and reliability is now nobody's job. r/SaaS: "Customer cancelled after 18 months. Reason: 'We built it ourselves.'", "No one is going to pay for your vibe-coded SaaS", "Mass-produced AI apps for 14 months. Made $2,847 total. My friend sells pool cleaning services and cleared $94K.", "I wasted $50k because I thought the code was the expensive part." r/Entrepreneur (88/100): "The SaaS model is quietly falling apart for small businesses." When the dispatch board or intake form breaks at 7am, nobody is answerable.
solution: 1) A one-click deploy of an AI-built app to a hardened runtime with auth, nightly backups, uptime checks, data export and secrets rotation. 2) Dependency and security patching. 3) A "break-glass" human fix within one business day, sold as credits. 4) Builders resell the bundle with their own markup, so they earn recurring revenue from boring customers instead of chasing SaaS signups. 5) The small business gets an SLA and a runbook in plain language.
why_now: In February 2026 nearly $1T was wiped from software and services valuations as coding agents made build-versus-buy tilt toward build (TechCrunch, Mar 1, 2026). Small customers are now building their own replacements, and thousands of AI-SaaS founders who cannot sell subscriptions are turning to service-style custom work.
revenue_model: $39-79 per app per month wholesale to builders, who charge clients $100-200/mo. Break-glass fix credits ($150 per incident). A $199/mo direct plan for owners who built their own tool.
non_obvious_insight: When code is cheap, the scarce thing is accountability: someone who answers when the tool breaks. The supply and demand are visible in the same threads: small customers churn because they built it themselves (r/SaaS, https://www.ideafast.pro/pains/saas), and r/Entrepreneur scores "The SaaS model is quietly falling apart for small businesses" at 88/100 (https://www.ideafast.pro/pains/Entrepreneur). The macro shift toward build over buy is documented at https://techcrunch.com/2026/03/01/saas-in-saas-out-heres-whats-driving-the-saaspocalypse/. Honest caveat: the demand for the caretaking layer is inferred from these signals, not seen in a direct "I'd pay for" post, so the first month is a paid-demand test.
first_30_days: Week 1: DM 30 builders who posted about pivoting to "boring" service customers, and offer to host and maintain their existing client apps for $49. Weeks 2-3: onboard 10 real apps onto a standard stack (managed database, backups, uptime monitor, alerts) using off-the-shelf tooling. Week 4: sell the wholesale plan to the first 3 builders and log every incident to price break-glass credits. Kill test: fewer than 5 paying apps after 30 days means the pain is not there.

title: Sworn Testator Depositions for the Deepfake Era
one_liner: Estate attorneys refer aging or blended-family clients to a 45-minute sworn Q&A on intent and capacity, taken by a reporter who certifies it and stored in an escrow vault that opens on death. Because a human certified it, it stays credible when video can be faked.
customer: Estate planning and elder law attorneys, whose clients pay $1,200-$3,000 per session (billed through as a cost). Also wealth advisors and family offices serving blended-family, dementia-risk or high-conflict heirs. Trust and estate litigators are a secondary buyer.
problem: The great wealth transfer is driving more will and trust contests over capacity and undue influence. The standard defense is a video of the signing, but anyone can now claim video or audio is synthetic or edited. Attorney file notes look self-serving, and witness memory fades over the 5-15 years between signing and death. Court reporters are the one neutral officer who can administer an oath and certify a verbatim record. Only litigation agencies dispatch reporters, so estate lawyers never think to hire one.
solution: A productized package. A licensed reporter administers the oath. The attorney or an independent examiner runs a structured interview covering assets, family, reasons for unequal splits, and awareness of who might object. An optional treating-physician attestation is added. The client receives a certified transcript, hash-locked and time-stamped video, and the reporter's certificate. Everything goes into an encrypted escrow vault that releases on a death certificate or an attorney trigger. Clients re-sit every 2-3 years. The package maps to ante-mortem probate options in the few states that have them (Ohio and Alaska are examples) and to each state's rules for perpetuating testimony. Admissibility varies by jurisdiction, so attorneys own the legal strategy.
why_now: Deepfakes are making courts wary of unauthenticated audio and video. The federal Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules was still working on a Rule 901(c) deepfake amendment and a new Rule 707 for machine-generated evidence at its October 2026 meeting. Remote depositions and remote-reporting laws such as California's AB 3013 make flexible scheduling normal, and estate sessions can be scheduled unlike litigation work. The wealth transfer is under way now.
revenue_model: $1,200-$3,000 per session, with about 50-60% going to the reporter. Vault fee of about $150 per year. $600 re-sit sessions every 2-3 years, which creates a recurring long tail. No referral fees to attorneys, because ethics rules prohibit fee splitting. Attorneys bill the session as a case cost.
non_obvious_insight: The reporter's certificate and oath are the one part of a transcript AI cannot counterfeit, and its value rises as media authenticity falls. Estate planners sit outside the reporter dispatch network, so nobody has packaged the reporter's authority for them.
first_30_days: Partner with 2 licensed reporters and 1 estate attorney, ideally in a large metro or an ante-mortem-probate state. Write the interview protocol with the attorney and a geriatric psychiatrist consultant. Offer a free pilot to 10 estate and elder-law firms through bar CLE lunches and local ACTEC chapters, targeting one blended-family client each. Aim for 5 paid sessions by day 30.

title: Mod-Approved Human Panels for Rare Audiences
one_liner: A research-recruitment service that turns Reddit's hardest-to-reach niche communities into bot-proof, mod-approved survey panels, with participants paid directly and the community getting the results back.
customer: UX and market research teams at health-tech, B2B SaaS and pharma patient-insights groups, boutique research agencies, and academic labs that need rare respondents (night-shift nurses, HVAC techs, POTS patients, first-time landlords, small-farm owners). Projects run $3k-$25k.
problem: Mainstream panels are being contaminated. A PNAS paper showed an autonomous AI survey respondent passing 99.8% of 6,000 standard attention checks. Rare-audience recruiting already costs $100-$300+ per complete and is slow. Researchers try recruiting in subreddits, but mods delete nearly every third-party survey post because of spam, data-harvesting fears, no ethics statement, no give-back, and no sample cap. Researchers get banned, and mod teams drown in survey modmail.
solution: A standardized 'research request kit': ethics and data-handling statement, incentive amount, sample cap, screener, and a commitment to post a plain-language results summary back to the community. Mods get a free Devvit intake queue with a checklist so approval takes about 60 seconds. Participants are paid directly (gift cards or PayPal), and nothing is paid to mods or communities, which respects Rule 5. Respondents can opt in to prove community tenure through user-consented OAuth (account age and history in that sub) plus a short liveness check and behavioral AI-agent detection. Buyers get a fraud-audit report with the data.
why_now: Agentic AI now beats standard survey quality checks (PNAS, late 2025), and research teams are actively looking for provably human samples. Reddit's five-community moderator cap, enforced from 31 March 2026, has thinned experienced mod teams, so requests that arrive pre-vetted and standardized are far more likely to be approved than cold modmail.
revenue_model: Per-complete pricing of $40-$150 (participant incentive $15-$60, gross margin roughly 35-45%), a $1.5k recruitment setup fee per project, annual retainers for repeat research teams, and a paid 'verified human' audit add-on.
non_obvious_insight: A mod team's approval plus demonstrable community tenure is a stronger anti-bot screen than any attention check, because aged, niche-active accounts are expensive to fake at scale and community norms punish liars. Mods say no for three fixable reasons (no results back, no data promises, no cap), so fixing those makes them say yes. The buyer's real pain isn't cost per complete but the fear that their data is silently synthetic.
first_30_days: Write the request kit and a one-page ethics template. Recruit 10 mid-size niche mod teams (10k-300k members) through mod Discords and existing goodwill, offering the intake queue free. Land 3 paid pilots from UX consultancies or academic labs at a 30% discount in exchange for case studies. Run three studies of about 100 completes each. Publish a side-by-side fraud audit against a conventional panel sample. Review Reddit's Data API commercial terms first, and keep responses collected off-platform.

title: Slop-Risk Diligence for Creator-Business Buyers
one_liner: A fixed-price quality-of-earnings report that prices the platform-policy cliff hiding inside a YouTube channel, newsletter or podcast network for sale.
customer: Search funds, micro-PE roll-ups, creator funds and revenue-based lenders acquiring channels, newsletters and podcast networks priced at roughly $200k-10M, and the brokers who sell them.
problem: Buyers price trailing-12-month revenue. But YouTube's Jul 16 clarification demonetizes generic or repetitive content and AI personas on finance, legal and health topics, Snap stopped recommending fully-AI content, and LinkedIn added a slop-report button. A channel can look healthy on the last year's statements and be one policy update from losing its income. Traditional QoE providers and listing brokers do not model this risk.
solution: A five-day diligence package: audit of how content is produced (share of AI scripts, voices and visuals, template repetition measured via embeddings, reused and stock footage), a policy-risk score against current platform rules, revenue concentration, copycat and re-post exposure, strike and claim history, and an 'earnings at risk' range with suggested earn-out triggers. Templated pipeline with analyst review.
why_now: Creator M&A and creator funds are growing (Slow Ventures' $60M creator fund, brokered channel sales), and the July 2026 policy clarifications make the next 12 months structurally different from the last 12.
revenue_model: $2.5-7.5k per report (roughly 1% of deal size), fund subscriptions for 10+ reports a year, and $500/month post-close earn-out monitoring.
non_obvious_insight: Diligence prices the past, and the AI-slop rules make the coming year differ from the past one. Policy risk is a new line in an existing budget, so no new budget is needed.
first_30_days: Pull 50 public listings from Flippa, Empire Flippers and Acquire. Publish five free teardowns, then sell $2.5k reports to buyer communities and search-fund Slack groups.

title: Referee Body-Cams and Abuse Evidence Layer
one_liner: A clip-on camera and incident-report service that gives youth and high school officials proof and gives leagues grounds to ban abusive spectators.
customer: State high school associations, officials' associations, youth leagues and tournament operators, paying per official per season.
problem: About 50,000 high school officials have left since 2018, more than 70 percent of new referees quit within three years, and half report feeling unsafe. Insiders assume pay raises fix the shortage, but abuse is the driver and leagues cannot sanction parents or coaches without evidence, so games run short-staffed or get cancelled.
solution: A $50-100 chest-mounted camera or phone clip with audio; speech-to-text flags threats and slurs; league admins get a one-click incident packet (timestamps, transcript, clip) tied to a spectator code of conduct; officials get a private 'safe report' button. Leagues use the evidence to issue bans and support refs.
why_now: 2026 shortage coverage (New York, Utah and others) consistently blames abuse; cheap on-device transcription and body cams make this a $60 problem; national bodies such as USA Volleyball have created formal harassment-response programs, showing appetite.
revenue_model: $40-90 per official per season (hardware included) plus $500-3k per year per league for the admin dashboard; potential insurer partnerships.
non_obvious_insight: The shortage is a safety problem, not a pay problem, and the true buyer is the league's risk manager. Recording laws vary by state, so the product is policy-first (posted notices, opt-in associations) and starts where the association mandates it.
first_30_days: Pilot with one regional officials association (about 100 officials) using off-the-shelf action cams and a transcription pipeline, draft a spectator-policy template with a local attorney, run one season of evidence, and convert two leagues into paying customers.

title: GitHub Outage Hot-Standby Forge
one_liner: A managed Forgejo standby that continuously mirrors repos, PRs, issues and Actions workflows, runs monthly failover drills, and lets a team ship a hotfix in minutes when GitHub is down, so nobody has to migrate off GitHub.
customer: Engineering teams of 5-200 with on-call rotations and release SLAs (B2B SaaS, fintech, agencies), plus EU firms who want a sovereignty story. They pay $8-12 per developer per month, or $99/month flat for teams of 10 or fewer.
problem: Ask HN 'Alternatives to GitHub' hit 649 points and 437 comments on 17 August 2026: 'Github has been down consistently over the last few months'; one team 'had to delay a release due to Github being down'; another said GitHub exceeded in two months a downtime budget its self-hosted GitLab had used only 1.5 days of in six years. The blockers cited for actually leaving are GitHub Actions lock-in, the PR workflow and ecosystem, not git hosting. Teams that do leave need 1-3 people to run a forge.
solution: A GitHub App that syncs code, tags, releases, and (read-write for a defined subset) PRs and issues into a managed per-customer Forgejo instance. A workflow portability linter tells the customer which of their Actions workflows will fail on Forgejo runners and proposes patches. Secrets are synced opt-in and encrypted. A break-glass switch redirects the deploy pipeline to standby runners (Forgejo v15 runs Kubernetes-native ephemeral runners). Monthly automated fire drills execute the customer's real deploy against staging in standby and produce a dated 'last successful failover' badge and status page for customers' security questionnaires.
why_now: GitHub instability through 2026, Forgejo Actions now described by users as 'near 1:1' with GitHub Actions, Forgejo v15's runner improvements (August 2026), and an AI-coding PR and CI volume surge that makes every hour of downtime costlier.
revenue_model: Per-developer subscription ($8-12/dev/month), $99/month flat for small teams, plus runner-minute overage and an enterprise tier with EU-only hosting and SSO.
non_obvious_insight: The 437-comment thread is framed as 'leave GitHub', but the stated blockers mean most teams will not, so the product that gets paid for is insurance rather than migration. Insurance is priced on drill evidence: a dated failover-drill badge is what a CTO can show a customer's procurement team. The open-source workflow linter is the wedge. Evidence: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49331033 (outage complaints, Actions as primary blocker, 'delay a release'); Forgejo Actions compatibility claims and DIY setups costing $60/month for a Kubernetes cluster https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48473170 and https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49360197.
first_30_days: Release a free open-source CLI that scores a repo's Actions workflows for Forgejo portability and post it in the GitHub-alternatives thread. Stand up a multi-tenant Forgejo with mirror sync in a few weeks using existing Forgejo, its runner and a sync service. Offer a $99/month founding-customer plan to the commenters who delayed releases and to 20 SaaS teams with uptime SLAs. Run the first joint failover drill with each design partner in week 4.

title: Savings-Group Credit Score and Treasury
one_liner: Turn informal savings groups into a credit bureau and stablecoin treasury that asset financiers can lend against.
customer: Financiers of productive assets (solar irrigation, motorbikes, milk coolers) and NGOs, with savings groups as end users.
problem: Sandi AI already reaches 10,000+ farmer groups that buy solar irrigation from pooled savings rather than loans. Chamas, VSLAs, tandas and arisan have no records that lenders can see.
solution: A WhatsApp and USSD ledger that logs contributions and minutes, produces a group credit history and optionally holds a stablecoin group treasury that diaspora members can top up. The wedge is selling qualified-group leads to asset financiers.
why_now: Kenya and Nigeria are legitimising stablecoins, local-language voice models can log minutes, and Sandi AI has shown demand.
revenue_model: $20-60 per funded asset lead, plus a 0.5% treasury fee.
non_obvious_insight: The group is the unit of trust in informal finance. Digitising it creates a bureau that cannot be scraped from mobile money data.
first_30_days: Sign 100 groups in Kenya through one NGO and record three months of contributions to prove predictive value.

title: Shared-Aide Pods for 55+ Apartment Buildings
one_liner: One on-site aide team serves 6-10 residents in the same building, delivering assisted-living-style help at a fraction of 1:1 home-care cost.
customer: Owners and operators of independent-living and 55+ apartment buildings (market-rate, senior LIHTC and HUD-202 properties). The payers are middle-income residents and their families, who can't afford $75-130k a year and are stuck on waitlists.
problem: Home care is sold as one aide per client per hour ($35 an hour, about $80k a year for 44 hours a week) only because of legacy billing. Assisted living is at 90% occupancy with almost no new supply before 2030. Residents who age past independent living either move out or go without.
solution: A licensed home-care agency subsidiary (or partnership with one) posts 2-3 aides per shift inside the building. They run scheduled 15-45 minute ADL, medication-reminder, meal-setup and toileting visits, plus overnight response. Dispatch software handles acuity tiers and in-building routing (floors, elevators). Residents buy monthly tiers of about $1,800-3,500, and the property gets a retention amenity.
why_now: NIC MAP shows 57 of 99 metros above 90% occupancy, units under construction at a 2012 low, and no meaningful new supply before 2030. Medicaid HCBS is walled off by 15-month waitlists and labor is scarcer after the 2026 visa pause, so stretching each aide across more clients is the only lever left.
revenue_model: Monthly resident subscription by care tier, with a revenue share or amenity fee to the property owner. Later, Medicaid HCBS or managed-care billing for pods in affordable senior buildings.
non_obvious_insight: Aide hours are cheap to make dense (no drive time, no client-hour minimums) but are priced as if they were mobile. The gap between 1:1 pricing and 1:8 cost is the whole business, and only a property-anchored operator can capture it. Assisted-living-without-the-license is a real category nobody has scaled.
first_30_days: Sign a 90-day pilot with one 100-200 unit 55+ property in a tight market. Subcontract to an existing licensed agency to move quickly, staff a two-aide pod, and target 15 residents at about $2,200 a month. Track aide minutes per resident and move-out avoidance.

title: Walkable Childhood Homes for Memory Care
one_liner: Generate explorable 3D versions of a person's childhood street, lost home or homeland from a few photos and stories, delivered on a TV or tablet for memory care, hospice and diaspora families.
customer: Memory-care and assisted-living communities (activity budgets), hospices and adult children, paying $250-600 per scene or $300-600 a month per community.
problem: Reminiscence is among the best-supported non-drug interventions for dementia and late-life low mood, but the props are still photos and music. Existing VR programs offer generic 'visit Paris' content, not personal places. Immigrants, refugees and the bereaved have no visual way back to a home that no longer exists.
solution: A studio workflow: family interview intake, photo and archival-map collection, a world-model pipeline that builds an era-appropriate walkable scene, and a docent mode where staff or grandchildren ask 'what was on this corner?'. Human artists finalize each scene to remove uncanny or distressing artifacts, and a gentle mode limits sensory intensity.
why_now: Generative world models released in 2025 (Google's Genie 3, World Labs' Marble and similar) can create persistent, explorable scenes from a handful of images. That cuts the cost of a personalized environment from thousands of dollars to well under $100 of compute.
revenue_model: Per-scene fees, community subscriptions for scene libraries and refreshes, hospice partnerships, and a consumer gift channel for diaspora families.
non_obvious_insight: Reminiscence works best when it is specific and shared, and personalization used to cost too much. The most valuable scenes are not beautiful cities but the ordinary corner, kitchen and street a person actually lived on.
first_30_days: Offer 10 memory-care communities three free scenes each, generated from residents' family photos. Track engagement and agitation logs with staff, then sell five-scene packs at $500 and add one hospice partner.

title: Micro-Bounties for Humans to Rescue Stuck Robots
one_liner: An on-demand app where robots and AVs post 30-second physical tasks (close a door, plug in a charger, move a cone, lift a robot over a curb) and nearby humans get paid instantly.
customer: Operators of sidewalk delivery robots, robotaxi and AV fleets, drone hubs, cleaning robots and warehouse AMRs, paying about $3-15 per task.
problem: Autonomy fails at the last physical one percent. Only 54% of Waymo's first 86M miles carried a passenger and each reset cycle takes about 2 hours. Dispatching a staffer or tow costs far more than the fix, and each fleet builds its own field-ops team.
solution: An SDK in which the robot emits a help request with location, photos and a vision-language-model task description. Nearby vetted people accept it, the robot's own sensors verify completion, and payout is instant. Strict safety rules prevent anyone touching moving machines. Start with door-ajar, debris and stuck-at-curb tasks.
why_now: Robot fleets are scaling faster than field crews (Waymo about 500k rides a week, sidewalk fleets in the thousands), and AV firms have reportedly begun paying gig workers for simple physical fixes. Vision-language models can now write the task description automatically.
revenue_model: 20-30% take on each task plus a monthly platform fee per fleet.
non_obvious_insight: Every robot fleet needs a thin, geographically spread hands-and-feet layer that scales with robot count. A two-sided micro-labor network is cheaper than dedicated field teams, and because the robot is the buyer, demand is programmable and grows with every deployment.
first_30_days: Pick one metro with a delivery-robot or campus-robot operator, recruit 50 local gig workers, and dispatch manually by SMS. Sign a $2k a month pilot with a small fleet, run 500 tasks, and publish resolution-time data.

title: Emeritus: Paying 80-Year-Old Tradespeople for Tacit Knowledge
one_liner: Recruit retired machinists, lineworkers, boiler operators and railroad and telephone technicians in their 70s-90s, pay them hourly to teach on camera, and sell the corpus to AI labs, robotics companies and industrial firms.
customer: Robotics and embodied-AI labs, LLM data buyers who have exhausted white-collar experts, and utilities and plants that run 1970s-era equipment.
problem: The last generation with hand skills and legacy-system judgment is disappearing. Companies try to capture knowledge from employees before retirement with KM software, but the deepest experts left years ago and can't be reached by enterprise tools. AI labs pay $75-200+/hr to lawyers and doctors through Mercor and Surge but have thin coverage of physical-process knowledge. Retirees are invisible to gig platforms.
solution: A field-producer model. Partner with union retiree clubs, trade associations and retiree chapters (IBEW, IAM, railroad retiree groups). Send a two-person crew with a phone rig and lav mics to sit with each retiree in their garage, shop or a plant visit. Run structured 'teach-back' sessions on failure modes, sounds, smells and shortcuts. Transcribe, segment and tag with AI. Pay the expert $60-120/hr plus a royalty share when the corpus is licensed. Sell curated, rights-cleared datasets and 'ask the old-timer' search seats to plants.
why_now: AI labs are spending heavily on expert data (Mercor reportedly pays contractors about $1.5M a day), and humanoid and robotics teams need process knowledge. About 40% of the manufacturing workforce is retirement-eligible within a decade, and utilities report up to half pension-eligible by 2027. Multimodal models can now ingest video and audio at scale.
revenue_model: Dataset licensing per hour of tagged, rights-cleared sessions ($500-2,000/hr). Enterprise capture projects ($30-150k). Per-seat search and Q&A licenses. Expert royalties are a cost of goods, which is also the recruiting pitch.
non_obvious_insight: The scarcest expert data isn't PhDs but the 82-year-old who can diagnose a turbine by sound. Retirees are also the only experts with no employer NDA or IP claim, so their data rights are cleaner and they can sign licenses directly. For the elder, it is paid, respected work and social contact, which is what tech never offers 80-year-olds.
first_30_days: Pick one niche (say retired tool-and-die makers or utility lineworkers) and recruit through three retiree-association newsletters. Pay 15 experts $100/hr for 2-hour sessions and produce about 30 hours. Have a lawyer draft consent and licensing contracts with cognitive-capacity safeguards and a family representative. Send samples to 3 robotics companies and 2 utilities.

title: Physical-Properties Index for Every SKU
one_liner: A shared 'Gracenote for grasping': weight, center of mass, deformability, best grip points and packaging traits for millions of SKUs, sold to pick-robot makers and brands.
customer: Pick-and-pack robot vendors, 3PLs running robotic induction, CPG and retail brands (for robot-ready packaging certification), and humanoid developers.
problem: Picking robots fail on the long tail because they meet every SKU cold, and brands change packaging without notice. Amazon knows internally, but everyone else relearns per site.
solution: Fill the index from two sources: a scanning rig at partner 3PLs (3D scan, mass, center of mass, slip tests) and give-to-get contributions from robot fleets reporting grasp outcomes. Serve it by GTIN through an API with recommended grasp points and packing advice, and offer brands a 'Robot-Ready' grade that 3PLs reward with lower handling fees.
why_now: Robotic picking is now at scale (Amazon 1M+ robots, Symbotic $2.25B revenue, Maven-style mixed palletizing), and foundation models can use priors like these. A market of data buyers already exists.
revenue_model: API fees per lookup or per robot per month, $2-10k per SKU family for brand certification, and dataset licensing to model labs.
non_obvious_insight: Robots will not scale on smarter grasping alone. The world's goods need a machine-readable physical spec, and brands have a direct incentive because 3PLs and retailers will reward robot-ready packaging. A neutral index can become a standard the way GS1 barcodes did.
first_30_days: Build a $15k scanning rig at a friendly 3PL and scan the top 3,000 SKUs. Release a free tier, sign 2 pick-robot vendors as beta partners, and run one paid brand packaging audit.

title: Outside-Processing Milk Run for Job Shops
one_liner: Scheduled pickup routes and batching software for the heat-treat, plating and anodize bottleneck behind reshored machining.
customer: 10-100 person machine shops and fabricators, plus special-process houses (heat treat, anodize, plating, passivation, paint) that want fuller batches.
problem: As machining orders rise (machinery jobs +6.1k in August, record capital-goods orders), the constraint moves downstream to special processes. Shops ship parts by carrier ad hoc, parts sit in queues, and paperwork gets lost. ISM supplier deliveries have slowed for eight straight months. Environmental cost and owner retirements limit new special-process capacity (my inference).
solution: Vans on fixed weekly or daily routes between shops and vetted process vendors. Batching gives vendors full loads. Barcode chain of custody carries cert paperwork (heat-treat charts, NADCAP status). A promised turnaround (for example 5 days) is tracked by software.
why_now: Reshoring in existing walls raises job counts while outside-process capacity has not grown. Slowing deliveries make lead time visible.
revenue_model: Per-stop fee plus 8-12% margin on outside-processing volume. Vendor SaaS. Later, acquire a heat-treat or anodize house.
non_obvious_insight: Outside processing often accounts for most of a job's elapsed lead time but only a small share of touch time. That bottleneck yields to logistics and batching, not new furnaces, and adding a van is cheaper than adding an oven.
first_30_days: Pick one region such as Grand Rapids, Greenville or Wichita. Interview 20 shops. Sign two heat-treat or anodize houses. Run a one-van pilot two days a week and charge per stop.

title: Independent Auditor of Real Agent-Commerce Volume
angle: Pairing 1: AI agents & agent economy x Finance
one_liner: A neutral measurement firm that separates real agent payments from wash trading and testing, then sells diligence to investors and behavioral AML monitoring to the trust banks that carry the flows.
customer: Investors and acquirers diligencing agent-payment startups, protocol foundations and ecosystem funds that allocate grants on volume, OCC-chartered trust banks, stablecoin issuers and MSBs onboarding agent-wallet fintechs, and card networks and acquirers.
problem: Bloomberg found that about $24M of on-chain agent commerce shrinks to about $1.6M once self-trading wallets are removed, and Base logged about 97M protocol transactions with no one able to say how many were live. Meanwhile Tempo raised $500M and every network is announcing agent rails. KYC at onboarding does not fit wallets that act autonomously, and continuous behavioral KYC is the flagged gap.
solution: Cluster wallets, detect self-dealing, and classify each flow as test, wash or real economic activity (unique counterparties, fiat off-ramps, merchant tie-outs) across x402, MPP and AP2 settlement. Publish a free index, sell diligence reports, and offer an agent-tuned monitoring API that scores velocity, counterparty concentration and sanctions-adjacent exposure for BSA/AML programs.
why_now: x402 moved to the Linux Foundation in April 2026 and MPP is live. The Fed proposed GENIUS Act issuer rules on 2026-09-24, and OCC trust charters are being handed out (Circle on 2026-07-10, Coinbase in April, Bridge conditionally). A Senate report alleging about $2B of Iran-linked Tether flows raises the cost of weak compliance.
revenue_model: Diligence engagements at $15-60k each, monitoring subscriptions at $5-30k per month per bank or issuer, and data licensing to funds and networks.
non_obvious_insight: In a hype market the scarce good is credible measurement, and a firm with no token or protocol stake is the only party everyone can trust. The clustering work that debunks the volume numbers is the same compliance product regulated banks will have to buy, and it needs both on-chain forensics and agent-protocol fluency.
first_30_days: Two on-chain analysts build the wash filter on public data (Dune or Flipside), publish 'Real vs Reported Agent Commerce' with an open methodology, and pitch it to 15 funds and 3 foundations. Charge for the first bespoke diligence report within the month, and let the free index drive inbound.

title: End-of-Life Pet Cell Banking via Aftercare Providers
angle: Pairing 2: Biotech tools/synbio/lab automation/AI drug discovery x Pets & animal health/vet shortage/pet insurance
one_liner: Sell a living-cell keepsake through pet crematories and euthanasia vets, and build a consented canine and feline cell-and-genome atlas for research.
customer: Grieving pet owners pay $249-399 per animal. Pet crematories, in-home euthanasia vets and cemeteries are distribution partners. Vet-pharma, AI-drug-discovery and academic groups license the consented, de-identified cell lines and genomes.
problem: Owners will pay for memorials, but the only 'living' option today is boutique cloning-linked gene banking at roughly $1,600+ that almost nobody hears about at the moment they need it. Aftercare providers touch millions of pets a year and have no biotech product. At the same time, AI-driven and vet drug discovery lack breed-annotated cell lines and genomes tied to full medical histories, and proprietary biological datasets are commanding large valuations (Basecamp raised $140M; Tempus is assembling 100k genomes).
solution: A low-cost collection kit (skin punch biopsy in transport medium, chilled shipping) handled by a vet or trained aftercare staff within 24-48 hours of death. A contract lab establishes and cryopreserves fibroblast lines for 20+ years, and optional whole-genome sequencing is included. Owners choose 'keep only' or a discounted 'keep and donate to research'. Consented lines plus medical-record metadata go into a research atlas that partners license.
why_now: High-profile celebrity pet cloning in late 2025 made living pet genetics a mainstream conversation. Whole-genome sequencing now costs roughly $100-200, and proprietary datasets are what AI-bio investors pay for. Pet aftercare is a large, emotionally trusted channel that no biotech has approached, and vet-shortage-driven consolidation is pushing clinics toward add-on revenue.
revenue_model: $249-399 per animal plus $60 per year storage. Partners earn $40-60 per kit. Research licensing of consented lines and genomes at $500-2,000 per line with metadata, plus dataset subscriptions. Unit costs are about $120-180 for culture and cryostorage.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource for pet biotech is not technology but trusted access to animals at the moment of death, and that access sits with crematories and euthanasia vets, not labs. Framing the purchase as optionality (cloning, future cell therapy) plus a donation option turns a grief moment into a data flywheel.
first_30_days: Contract an academic or commercial cell-banking lab for a validated tissue-to-line protocol. Sign 3-5 pet crematories or in-home euthanasia practices in one metro, and place 20 kits at a $99 introductory price. Recruit a supervising veterinarian and create an owner consent form covering research use. Take the first 30-50 lines to two vet-pharma or AI-biotech prospects for a data pilot.

title: Powered Public Land Brokerage for Robotaxi Depots
angle: Pairing 2: Logistics & physical automation x Government/defense/municipal
one_liner: A broker that matches autonomous-fleet operators to cities' already-energized, under-used land such as transit depots, fleet yards and city garages, on leases that trade concessions cities value.
customer: Robotaxi, autonomous delivery-van and driverless-truck operators pay success fees and retainers (Waymo, Zoox, May Mobility, Avride, Gatik and others). Cities and transit agencies are the counterparty, earning lease income.
problem: Depot power is the choke point for scaling robotaxis. A standard California charging site takes about 6 months, a new circuit 1.9 years, a substation upgrade 2.8 years and a new substation 8.9 years, and depots now compete with data centers for powered industrial land. Waymo's first 86M miles were only 54% passenger-carrying, so depots and reset cycles matter more than vehicles. AV operators do not know which public parcels are already energized, because they sit in transit-agency asset registers rather than commercial real estate databases.
solution: Build a dataset of municipally owned parcels with existing high-capacity service: bus depots, municipal fleet yards, park-and-ride lots, closed school-bus yards, airport lots and city garages. Overlay it with utility load-capacity maps. Use a template 'public benefit lease' (revenue share, 24/7 emergency access, data sharing, wheelchair-accessible service commitments, local cleaning and charging jobs) so cities can say yes without a full RFP. Then broker the deals.
why_now: Waymo raised $16B at a $126B valuation in Feb 2026 and is expanding across 10-14 metros. Zoox began charging fares on Aug 10, 2026, Tesla is running unsupervised in two states, and Aurora is exiting 2026 with 200 driverless trucks that need terminals. Large-load grid queues are freezing in Texas, so already-energized land is worth years.
revenue_model: A success fee of 3-5% of lease value or $75-150k per signed site, plus $10-20k/month retainers from fleets that want a standing pipeline. Optional revenue share with the city.
non_obvious_insight: The scarcest input for autonomous-fleet scale is already-energized land, not compute or vehicles, and the largest holder of it is city government. City government cannot run a competitive marketplace but values non-cash concessions (accessibility, data, jobs) that a private landlord never offers.
first_30_days: In Texas, Arizona and Georgia metros with announced AV expansions, file public-records requests for depot and yard inventories plus utility service sizes. Build a 100-parcel shortlist. Pitch three fleet real-estate leads a paid $25k 'top-10 sites' report.

title: Privacy-Compliant Monetization for Faith Apps
angle: Pairing 1: Legal services, compliance & new regulations (EU AI Act, privacy, PFAS, right to repair, etc.) x Weird, niche and overlooked markets (hobbies, collectibles, faith communities, subcultures)
one_liner: An audit-plus-replacement stack for small prayer, Quran, Bible, Torah and temple apps whose ad SDKs quietly turn every user into a sale of religious-belief data.
customer: Independent and mid-size publishers of ad-funded faith apps (prayer times, Quran, Bible/devotional, Hindu calendar, Zmanim, halal finders, congregation apps) and church-management/giving software vendors serving thousands of congregations.
problem: Religious beliefs are special-category data under GDPR Art. 9 and 'sensitive data' requiring opt-in consent under nearly every US state privacy law. Maryland's law goes further, banning the sale of sensitive data and limiting collection to what is strictly necessary (in force since Oct 2025, verify enforcement dates). Regulators have treated mere use of a niche app as revealing sensitive traits (Norway's Grindr fine, upheld on appeal, verify). Reporting in 2020 showed a Muslim prayer app's location data reaching a broker and then US military contractors. Yet most small faith apps run stock ad SDKs with device IDs and location, have no consent flow and no counsel. The briefing notes non-Christian faith apps are far less served than Hallow-style Christian ones, and the IAPP says state privacy momentum is at an all-time high.
solution: (1) A public audit tool that scans app binaries and web properties for SDK data flows and issues a scorecard plus a legal-risk memo by state and EU. (2) A drop-in compliance SDK: a consent manager that treats every user as sensitive by default, server-side region logic, data maps and DPIA templates in Arabic, Urdu, Bahasa, Hebrew, Spanish and Portuguese. (3) A contextual, ID-free sponsorship marketplace where halal, kosher, umrah, church-goods and faith-nonprofit sponsors book placements by content context (for example an iftar-times page). (4) A subpoena and data-request playbook with minimal retention by design, so the app has little to hand over.
why_now: State privacy laws with sensitive-data opt-in are now the norm and Maryland's strict rules are enforceable in 2026 (verify dates). GDPR fines total EUR 7.16B with 229 new cases in 2026 (per briefing). Faith apps are booming (Hallow reached #1 in the US App Store) while faith data is politically charged around surveillance and immigration enforcement.
revenue_model: $149-499/month per app for SDK plus audit. 25-30% revenue share on contextual sponsorship. One-time $1.5-3k audit and fix sprint. Enterprise contracts with church-tech vendors.
non_obvious_insight: For a faith app the category itself reveals the belief (the Grindr logic), so 'we do not collect religion' is not a defense. The violation is the ad model, so the fix is a different revenue stream, not a policy PDF. Contextual sponsorship from faith-community advertisers can pay better than junk programmatic. Public scorecards create the sales funnel, because in tight communities reputation and fear move fast.
first_30_days: Audit the top 100 Muslim prayer/Quran apps and 50 Christian, Jewish and Hindu apps with open-source traffic analysis (mitmproxy, Exodus-style trackers). Publish a 'Privacy Scorecard for Faith Apps' and email each publisher. Sell paid fix sprints to 5 pilot apps at about $2k and recruit 5 community sponsors for contextual placements. Team is one privacy lawyer plus one Android engineer.

title: Made-in-USA Proof Files for Relabeling Brands
one_liner: Audit-ready substantiation files and monitoring for brands rushing to claim 'Made in USA' after tariffs.
customer: Consumer and industrial brands with $5M-$300M revenue and retailer private-label teams, buying through general counsel or the ecommerce head.
problem: Tariffs make US-made claims valuable, but an unqualified 'Made in USA' claim needs 'all or virtually all' US content and processing under FTC rules, with civil penalties per violation and state-law class actions on top. Brands switch suppliers on cost and forget the claim. Suppliers cannot document origin per component.
solution: Software plus service that maps each SKU's BOM to component and labor origin, gathers supplier attestations and mill certs, scores the claim, drafts compliant packaging and listing language ('Assembled in USA with global parts', or percent US), monitors marketplace listings and supplier changes, and builds a defense binder.
why_now: A reshoring marketing wave, supplier switching under tariffs, and active enforcement risk. The same BOM data that supports tariff compliance supports the claim.
revenue_model: $3-15k per product-line audit plus $500-2k a month for monitoring. Retailer programs that require proof.
non_obvious_insight: The first legal casualty of the reshoring wave is the label. Brands that reshore partially and market fully carry hidden liability, and a file built once serves both marketing and customs defense. The buyer is legal or marketing, not customs, so this avoids the crowded tariff-software budget.
first_30_days: Scan Amazon 'Made in USA' listings for weak claims using public data. Send a three-page claim risk scorecard to the brands. Sell the first 10 audits at $3k with a partner advertising lawyer signing off.
